problem: The answer says unpooling loses exact positions. This contradicts Section 1, which correctly says unpooling uses switch positions saved during max pooling. Max pooling discards non-maximum values, not the positions of the selected maxima.
fix: No; max pooling discards non-maximum values, and ReLU/convolution also lose information, so the deconv reconstruction cannot recover exact pixel values. It shows evidence, not a perfect inverse.

where: Section 3, CAM definition and Exam traps
problem: CAM is defined with a ReLU: L^c = ReLU(Σ_k w_k^c A^k). In the standard CAM formulation, the class activation map is the weighted sum Σ_k w_k^c A^k. The ReLU belongs to Grad-CAM, or is an optional display post-process; the trap repeats it as required for CAM.
fix: Write CAM as L^c = Σ_k w_k^c A^k. Keep the ReLU in Grad-CAM: L^c = ReLU(Σ_k α_k^c A^k). If negatives are clamped for CAM display, call that optional post-processing.

problem: “Deconvolution, also called transposed convolution or backprop-to-image” conflates a layer with a visualization method. Backprop-to-image is the gradient of an activation with respect to the input; deconvolution is transposed convolution used inside a deconvnet.
fix: Say: “Deconvolution (transposed convolution) is the layer used in a deconvnet; backprop-to-image is a related gradient visualization method, not another name for the layer.”

problem: Says CAM needs “a specific pooling layer and retraining.” CAM needs a global average pooling layer; retraining is needed only if the trained model does not already have one.
fix: CAM needs a global average pooling layer, and retraining only if the model lacks one; Grad-CAM works on the existing model using gradients.
